analysis.one_liner: Requires big public companies that buy back their own stock to pay workers a cash dividend or owe an equal tax.
analysis.headline: The Worker Dividend Act of 2019 was introduced by a single House Democrat in September 2019, referred to the Ways and Means Committee, and died there with zero cosponsors and no hearing or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required large publicly traded companies to share buyback money with their workers. Whenever a company with over $250 million in U.S. profits spent cash repurchasing its own stock, it would have to pay every U.S. employee an equal cash "worker dividend" — on top of normal pay — or owe the Treasury a tax of the same amount. The bill never advanced past its committee referral.
analysis.who_benefits: U.S. employees of large publicly traded companies. If a covered employer bought back its own stock, each worker would receive an equal cash payment (part-timers pro rata for hours worked), paid within 60 days of year-end, and it could not be swapped for or deducted from existing compensation [S2, S3]. Companies could instead choose to make it a documented permanent raise in regular pay [S3]. Because the dividend is triggered by buybacks and tied to profits above $250 million, the biggest checks would flow at the most profitable large corporations [S2].
analysis.who_benefits_short: U.S. employees at large public companies

how_it_helps.text: Would have required any publicly traded employer that repurchases its own stock, and has more than $250 million in U.S. earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortization, to pay its U.S. employees a worker dividend equal to the lesser of the buyback amount or half the profits above that $250 million threshold.

Each employee would receive an equal payment, with part-time workers paid pro rata for hours worked, and the payment would be in addition to — not a substitute for — compensation the worker already receives.

Enforcement would be automatic: a company that skipped the dividend would owe the IRS a tax equal to the required dividend, and would have to report buybacks and dividend payments to the Treasury and the SEC.

analysis.who_pays: Large publicly traded companies and, by extension, their shareholders. A company could avoid the tax only by paying out cash to its workforce that it would otherwise have used to repurchase shares, so the cost lands on corporate treasuries and the shareholders who benefit from buybacks. Investors include ordinary people through 401(k)s and pensions, but the direct cost falls on the companies and the shareholders who gain most from buybacks.
analysis.who_pays_short: Large public companies and their shareholders

drawbacks.text: The mandate is blunt: it hits every public company with buybacks and over $250 million in U.S. profits, including ones with well-paid workforces, and its size is pegged to company profits rather than to how low wages actually are, so money could flow to already-comfortable employees at profitable firms rather than targeting the lowest-paid workers.

Buybacks return cash to shareholders, many of them ordinary people through retirement funds and pensions, and a standing requirement to redirect buyback cash to wages could make companies less willing to repurchase stock or could pressure them to reduce hiring or other costs to cover the payout.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: On its face the bill would have moved a share of buyback cash to workers at profitable companies, and the equal-payment rule plus the pay-on-top requirement were designed to keep companies from gaming it. But it was a one-size-fits-all mandate tied to profits and buybacks rather than to wage levels, so its benefits would be spread evenly across workforces, including well-paid ones, and its costs would fall on companies and their shareholders — including small investors — with no exemption for firms that already pay high wages. In practice the question never got tested: with no cosponsors and no committee action, the idea received no hearing, no refinement, and no vote.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never held a hearing or a markup, and the bill expired when the 116th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Joseph P. Kennedy III introduced the Worker Dividend Act of 2019 on September 19, 2019, and it was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means the same day.
No other member of the House cosponsored the bill, and the Ways and Means Committee took no further action on it — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — before the Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large publicly traded companies and their shareholders are better off, since no buyback-to-workers mandate was ever imposed; nothing about corporate buyback practice or worker pay changed.

for.name: Rep. Joseph P. Kennedy III
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to Ways and Means; recruited no cosponsors

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no action after referral — no hearing, no markup, no vote — for the rest of the Congress

against.name: Richard Neal
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for committee consideration during his chairmanship

against.name: House colleagues of both parties
against.what_they_did: No member signed on as a cosponsor, leaving the bill with no demonstrated support

sides.party_line_note: The bill never reached a vote and had a single Democratic sponsor with zero cosponsors from either party, so no partisan split on the merits was ever recorded.

industries.note: Any public company with over $250 million in U.S. profits that bought back its own stock would have owed either a worker dividend or an equal tax, forcing buyback cash into worker paychecks. The industry's interest in blocking the bill ran directly against the workers who would have received the payouts.

industries.industry: Shareholders, including mutual and pension funds
industries.note: Shareholders fund buybacks, so the mandate would have reduced the cash returned to them; but many shareholders are ordinary workers through 401(k)s and pensions, so the burden partly falls back on the people the bill aims to help.
A standing tax on buybacks that skip worker dividends would have made repurchases costlier and likely less frequent, reducing activity in the repurchase market.
